data.title: NeuroVista Labs Advances Neuroplasticity Drug Discovery Program with U.S. Market Focus
data.description:
CURITIBA, Brazil —

CURITIBA, Brazil, October 15, 2026 — NeuroVista Labs, a Brazilian biotechnology company developing a neuroplasticity-focused drug discovery program with the United States as its primary target market, today announced that its synthesized research compounds have advanced into in vitro testing in laboratories in Brazil.

The milestone moves the program from theoretical and computational research into experimental evaluation. The studies will investigate the compounds’ biological activity and generate evidence to guide subsequent development decisions.

Based in Curitiba, NeuroVista is conducting its research in Brazil while building a development strategy focused on the U.S. pharmaceutical market. The company aims to translate research conducted in Brazilian laboratories into drug development opportunities with international reach.

“We are building NeuroVista with a clear international direction: conducting research in Brazil while developing our program with the U.S. market as our primary focus,” said Ravi Kaiut, CEO and Lead Scientist of NeuroVista Labs. “Advancing from a hypothesis to synthesized compounds and laboratory testing gives us the opportunity to generate the experimental evidence needed to move that strategy forward.”

NeuroVista’s research focuses on neuroplasticity—the nervous system’s capacity to adapt and reorganize—as a foundation for investigating potential therapeutic approaches to neurological diseases.

The program began with a scientific hypothesis and computational research to inform compound design and selection. Following synthesis, the compounds are now undergoing in vitro evaluation in Brazil to assess whether their biological activity supports further development.

The program remains at an early stage of preclinical research. The compounds’ safety and efficacy in humans have not been established.

data.title: Biotech IPOs are the industry’s lifeblood. Track how they’re performing.
data.description:
Initial public offerings make the biotechnology industry tick. Stock listings give young companies the funding they need to develop their drugs, and their venture backers an opportunity to earn a return.

For much of the past decade, biotechs found Wall Street receptive to their pitches. Public investment, drawn in by scientific advances and company successes, bolstered generations of new drugmakers.

IPO activity reached a peak in 2021, when more than 100 biotechs priced an initial offering and together raised nearly $15 billion. But that momentum came to a halt in 2022 as stock prices of newly public companies plummeted amid a sector-wide downturn. The pace of IPOs stalled and, last year, only 11 drugmakers priced initial share sales.

Emerging biotechs now face a tougher road to public markets. Which will make it? Which create value and which fail? What types of companies earn the best returns? Who are their investors?

Biopharma Dive is tracking these questions in the database below, which will be updated regularly. If we've missed anything, or there's any additional information you'd like to see, please reach out and let us know.

data.title: Decreasing process variability in fluid management systems
data.description:
Connectivity represents something much larger than component compatibility. It is the foundation for standardization, predictability and control. Every connection influences whether a process can be reliably transferred, consistently executed and confidently scaled. When done right, early process decisions can translate to accelerated progress across development and scale‑up.

For organizations developing mAbs, mRNA therapies, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), multispecific antibodies and cell therapies—process robustness, technology transfer and manufacturing scalability increasingly rely on the effectiveness of single-use assemblies. Yet one factor remains consistently underestimated: physical connectivity or fluid management. The tubing, connectors, sensors and fluid transfer paths that link unit operations together can have a profound impact on flow behavior, process consistency, scalability and regulatory compliance.

As therapies become more complex and manufacturing networks expand across sites, every connection point in a process becomes a potential source of variability. These connectors are not merely passive components. Together, they define how material moves through a process, how consistently the process performs and how easily it can be transferred, replicated and scaled.

The challenge is that bioprocesses may evolve over time based on modality-specific requirements, which means incorporating new equipment or retrofitting technologies. A straightforward process can then become a patchwork of connection types, tubing dimensions, materials and supplier specifications. As manufacturers document deviations and are forced to troubleshoot flow inconsistencies and validate component changes, they’re left repeatedly asking the question, Why does this process behave differently here than it did there?

Physical connectivity is not simply about ensuring components fit together, it’s ensuring that the entire manufacturing system functions together. The performance of a process is influenced not just by a connector, tubing segment or flow kit, but by how all the elements of the fluid pathway interact as an integrated system. Small decisions made upstream can have significant consequences downstream. In this article, we discuss a few examples of why connectors can’t be chosen with only one piece of the process in mind.

End-to-end fluid management: why flow kits can’t be designed in isolation

In modern biomanufacturing, every transfer step must behave as expected. Unexpected flow behavior can result in batch delays, troubleshooting efforts, product loss or deviations that impact manufacturing efficiency. Yet flow path design decisions are often evaluated at the equipment level rather than at the process level. Because fluids do not recognize equipment boundaries, the performance of a flow kit is influenced by the entire transfer system surrounding it. Designing flow kits in isolation can therefore create hidden risks that are not discovered until the process is operating under real manufacturing conditions.

A common misconception in bioprocessing is that a flow kit can be designed around the requirements of the processing unit alone. The entire fluid transfer pathway within this skid, from the origin through the flow kit and to the destination, must be considered. Take, for example, a chromatography skid with a flow kit designed around a bore size of “X.” In chromatography, bore size refers to the internal diameter (ID) of the tubing. At first glance, it may seem reasonable to use X as the bore size through the system. However, many manufacturing facilities operate with long transfer distances between buffer preparation areas and process skids. Over those distances, pressure losses can become significant.

In these cases, MSAT and process engineers may intentionally specify a bore size larger than X, even though this is larger than the bore of the system flow path itself. The larger tubing diameter helps reduce pressure drop across long runs, minimizing the risk of cavitation, tubing collapse, pump performance issues and process interruptions.

A successful design requires consideration of the entire transfer pathway, including:

  • Mixer bag and tote outlet sizes
  • Tubing diameters across transfer distances
  • Transfer set configurations
  • Pump requirements
  • Pressure-drop limitations
  • Aseptic connector sizing
  • Final flow kit geometry

What appears to be a simple tubing selection decision is often a system-level engineering decision. For organizations seeking predictable manufacturing performance, every connection point must be considered within the context of the complete process. A well-designed fluid management strategy accounts not only for the flow kit itself, but also for the entire network of components that deliver fluid to and from the process (Fig 1).

 

Fig 1. Cytiva’s Batch 360™ service collaborates with you to design a single-use consumable package optimized for your end-to-end manufacturing workflow.

Many connectivity challenges are not discovered when a component is selected. They are discovered during scale-up, technology transfer or commercial manufacturing. Cytiva works alongside you to design, evaluate and optimize manufacturing systems with the goal of reducing complexity, improving standardization and creating more robust processes from development through commercial production. data.title: Integra Therapeutics strengthens executive leadership with the appointment of Simon Dew as Chief Business Officer
data.description:
BARCELONA, Spain —

Integra Therapeutics, a global leader in cutting-edge gene writing tools designed to improve the efficacy, precision and safety of advanced therapies, today announced the appointment of Simon Dew as Chief Business Officer (CBO). 

Mr. Dew brings extensive executive experience in business development and licensing, corporate strategy, portfolio planning, commercial development, alliance management, and investor relations. He joins Integra from Macomics Ltd., where he was responsible for developing and implementing a business plan for out licensing clinical assets and platform technology with the primary purpose of partnerships within biopharma and academia.

Previously, Mr. Dew served as Chief Business Officer at ReNeuron Plc; Vice President of Business and Corporate Development at Mereo BioPharma; Vice President of Business Development at Evox Therapeutics; Vice President of Corporate Strategy at Gyroscope Therapeutics (acquired by Novartis); and SVP Corporate Strategy and Communications at Astellas Pharma. Earlier in his career, he held positions as Project Director at GSK and Product Manager at Bristol Myers.

Mr. Dew completed an Executive Leadership Program at Duke University and holds a BSc in Pharmacy from the University of Portsmouth. He is a member of the Royal Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain.

“We are delighted to welcome Simon to our leadership team at such a pivotal time for Integra. His vast experience in business development and corporate strategy across cell and gene therapy, oncology, immunology, and rare diseases will be crucial as we enter our next phase of growth, building alliances with global industry leaders to maximize the reach and value of FiCAT,” said Avencia Sanchez-Mejias, PhD, CEO & Co-Founder of Integra Therapeutics.

“Integra has built a highly differentiated gene writing modular platform with the potential to improve the precision and scalability of cell engineering for next-generation CAR-T therapies,” said Mr. Dew. “The opportunity to help address some of the major limitations of current treatments, including severe toxicities, high costs, and manufacturing delays, is only the beginning. I’m thrilled to join Integra at this exciting stage and and to work with the team to build the partnerships that will bring FiCAT's potential to patients.’’

FiCAT platform for next-generation CAR-T therapies

FiCAT (Find‑Cut‑And‑Transfer) is a next generation gene writing platform developed by Integra Therapeutics that enables precise, efficient, stable insertion of DNA fragments of unparalleled size into a genome, in a single step without viral vectors dependancies. It combines a ‘find’ module based on CRISPR‑Cas to target a specific genomic site, with a ‘cut‑and‑transfer’ module derived from a engineered transposase to insert the new genetic material in ex vivo and in vivo cell therapy (CAR-T) and gene therapy. FiCAT can be delivered in a viral-free manner via LNP pre-loading, with demonstrated efficiency in several tissues and cells. It is currently in preclinical development for oncology, autoimmune and genetic diseases.

data.title: Biotech startups are built on venture capital. Track funding rounds here.
data.description:
Drug development is an expensive, risky endeavor. Biotechnology companies just starting out are many years away from seeing profits, if ever. So more often than not, a startup’s success turning science into medicines can come down to how much money it raises. That’s where venture capitalists step in, investing many millions of dollars for stakes in newly formed companies.

Young drugmakers rely on these private partners to survive until they can reach major milestones like entering clinical testing, or going public. And over the past two decades, they’ve had more and more help. The amount of money put into biotech has climbed considerably, resulting in the creation of hundreds of new companies.

Tracking that investment can reveal important patterns, showing how different drug types or diseases rise or fall out of favor with investors. BioPharma Dive built this database to help make that larger picture clear.

We’ve focused on a group of 26 venture capital firms that are highly active in creating new drug developers. In the database below, we’ve collected funding rounds involving those firms, a ledger of investment that we’ll update regularly.

If we’ve missed anything, or there’s additional information you’d like to see, please reach out and let us know.

Clicking any underlined term in the main database at right will filter by that term. Click the down arrow at far right to expand the information displayed for each round.

Methodology and limitations:

For this database, BioPharma Dive compiled venture fundraising rounds for private biotechnology companies developing human medicines. We screened for rounds involving at least one of a group of 26 highly active venture capital firms involved in company creation.

This group was selected by comparing data from SVB, HSBC, William Blair and Bay Bridge Bio that identified the most active biotech venture capital firms in 2023 and 2024 (SVB, HSBC, William Blair), 2022 (SVB), 2021 (SVB) and in 2018 to 2023 (Bay Bridge Bio). Investment activity in those lists was defined by the number of fundraising rounds in which each firm participated that year.

We then eliminated firms that were primarily a “crossover” investor. That yielded a list of 26 venture capital firms.

This core group of 26 firms is narrow by definition. But the activity of these firms provides a meaningful snapshot of investment trends in the industry. Over time, we plan to expand on this initial database by adding in more firms that meet our target focus.

This database is similarly limited by time. We focused on rounds that were completed and announced on or after Jan. 1, 2022. This captures a period of time in which the biotech sector experienced a downturn after a record high and the sector’s subsequent recovery. We also plan to add historical data from prior to Jan. 1, 2022 in later updates.

For each round identified, we collected information on the relevant company’s drugmaking modality and therapeutic area of focus, as well as the company’s stage of development and lead investors, if not one of the core group of 26 firms.

We generally used a company’s lead program to determine its modality, therapeutic area of focus and stage of development at the time of each round’s completion. The only exceptions to this are companies that inherited a late-stage candidate, but identified an earlier candidate as their priority and reason for raising funds. We categorized companies’ phase of development by the latest stage begun at the time of financing. So a company raising money to start a Phase 2 clinical trial that it hadn’t yet begun would be classified as in Phase 1.

The modalities listed are broadly defined and may not precisely describe an individual company’s experimental drug(s). They were chosen to better show overall trends in investment activity. “Drug discovery,” as a category, is meant to indicate those companies exploring new areas of science broadly, rather than focusing on a specific type of medicine.

Similarly, therapeutic areas cover a large number of diseases and, in some cases, such as with rare conditions, overlap with others. Common diseases that didn’t fit in the categories listed, such as those primarily affecting the heart, lungs, kidneys and endocrine system, were classified under “other.” When companies identified more than one therapeutic area with equal priority, we classified them as working on “multiple” therapeutic areas. Those that identified multiple areas, but prioritized one over others were classified under that priority area.

The nomenclature of venture capital rounds is fairly consistent, but some firms did not identify whether their round was seed or Series A, B, C, etc. In those cases, we classified the round as “undisclosed.” Extensions, expansions, or other add-on raises to an earlier Series round are noted, but not classified separately.

Nearly all rounds were announced in U.S. dollars. A handful were priced in euros or other foreign currencies, which we converted to dollars using exchange rate data from the relevant country’s central bank on the day the round was announced.

We organized rounds by the date they were announced, which in some cases is much later than when the round was actually raised if a company was initially operating in stealth. We did this for consistency, and to better match when a round’s existence was public knowledge. 

BioPharma Dive will update this database as rounds that meet our screening criteria are announced, but there may be some delay in when new rounds are added.

data.title: Welo Life Sciences Announces Glass PV for AI-Enabled Pharmacovigilance Case Translation
data.description:
NEW YORK —

Welo Life Sciences, a Welo Global brand, today announced Glass PV, an AI-enabled pharmacovigilance case translation platform. Glass PV turns scanned adverse event documents, including handwritten notes, mixed languages, and complex layouts, into translated PDFs in their structure at scale

According to Welo Life Sciences’ measurements across completed cases, close to 100% of cases are delivered within the required 12- or 24-hour regulatory window. The platform uses an all-inclusive, per-case pricing model to give customers greater cost predictability without separate translation, formatting, or project management fees.

Glass PV addresses a persistent challenge in pharmacovigilance: scanned safety case documents that contain handwritten notes, multiple languages, and complex layouts are hard to process at scale and speed. These documents can require manual transcription and coordination among translators, desktop publishing specialists, and project managers. Glass PV brings document intake, text extraction, expert review, translation, and layout reconstruction into a single AI-enabled workflow. Specialist linguists trained in safety narratives, case terminology, and adverse event reporting review the translation.

“Safety teams are working against regulatory clocks. They shouldn't need four people and a chain of emails to efficiently translate one scanned case with handwriting on the page,” said Cristina Pardo, General Manager of Welo Life Sciences. “Glass PV eliminates manual handoffs. You submit the case, and you get back a translated document with the layout intact.”

Glass PV maintains an audit trail of document changes and review decisions to support traceability, with enterprise single sign-on and role-based access controls to manage access. Data is processed within Welo Life Sciences’ secure infrastructure under a data processing agreement. The platform also provides configurable account workflows and supports translation in more than 300 languages. 

“We put our name on the clock and on the quality,” Pardo added. “Automation handles extraction and layout, specialist linguists who know safety narratives own the language, and every edit and decision is recorded. Any translation can be reopened and reviewed, and that is what accountability looks like in this space.”

For more information or to request a Glass PV demonstration, visit welolifesciences.com or contact [email protected].

data.title: INmune Bio Inc. and Quantum Computing Inc. Partner to Apply Quantum Optimization and AI to Advance Alzheimer’s Drug Research and Explore New Applications for XPro
data.description:
BOCA RATON, Fla. —
  • Collaboration combines INmune Bio's clinical research with QCi's  Dirac-3S quantum optimization machine to identify potential new treatment indications and biomarkers for XPro
  • Initial engagement marks QCi's first commercial customer in pharmaceutical and biotechnology markets, expanding the application of quantum computing to drug development

BOCA RATON, Fla. and HOBOKEN, N.J., FinanceWire, October 14, 2026 — INmune Bio Inc. (Nasdaq: INMB) and Quantum Computing Inc. (Nasdaq: QUBT) today announced a collaboration to apply quantum computing, artificial intelligence (AI) and data analytics to identify new potential applications for XPro (XPro1595), INmune Bio's investigational treatment for Alzheimer's disease and other disease conditions.

The collaboration brings together INmune Bio's data from pre-clinical research through four clinical trials and understanding of disease biology with QCi's Dirac-3S quantum optimization machine. Working with clinical and publicly available biomedical datasets, the companies intend to use quantum computing alongside AI and conventional data analytics to uncover relationships that could help find diseases driven by the same biology XPro targets, and to prioritize those with the greatest potential for success. 

The Stage 1 engagement represents QCi's first commercial customer in the pharmaceutical and biotechnology market. The agreement also provides options for additional work as INmune Bio advances its clinical development programs.

"We've built a large clinical dataset on Alzheimer’s and other diseases, backed by years of work with XPro," said David Moss, Chief Executive Officer of INmune Bio. "This collaboration allows us to examine patient populations and biomarkers most likely to predict responses by analyzing large data sets. We'll look for the diseases with the greatest potential for success, those whose human biology matches what we've already seen XPro do, starting with rare diseases where trials can be smaller, faster and more capital-efficient, and where qualifying pediatric approvals may earn a Priority Review Voucher."

Together, the companies will build on INmune Bio's research into XPro to explore where its approach to targeting inflammation may offer the greatest potential. XPro is designed to selectively inhibit soluble tumor necrosis factor (TNF), a protein involved in inflammation, while preserving other TNF functions important to the immune system. INmune Bio is investigating its potential in neurological and rare diseases where this targeted approach may offer a therapeutic benefit.

Using its Dirac-3S entropy quantum optimization machine alongside AI and conventional analytics, QCi will look for patterns and relationships across these datasets that could help researchers better understand treatment responses, identify promising patient populations and prioritize new indications for further study.

“This is a great example of what practical quantum computing can look like today,” said Yuping Huang, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of QCi. “INmune Bio has a complex scientific problem and a substantial body of clinical and biological data. Our job is to bring new computing capabilities to that problem and see what we can learn. The potential to help researchers make better decisions about future treatments is exciting, and it opens an important new market for QCi.”

An important part of the program will be testing where quantum optimization adds value. The companies plan to compare results from QCi's quantum optimization machine with appropriate conventional statistical and machine-learning methods, evaluating which approaches are best suited to different parts of the analysis.

The work is also intended to establish a repeatable discovery process through quantum computing that INmune Bio can use with additional datasets and potential disease indications. 

For INmune Bio, the collaboration offers a new way to evaluate the broader potential of XPro and prioritize future development opportunities. For QCi, it represents an opportunity to showcase how its room-temperature, low-power quantum computing technology can be applied to complex, real-world problems in pharmaceutical research.

data.title: CRIO's new AI eSource Builder speeds up study builds while keeping site teams in control
data.description:
BOSTON —

CRIO, the leading provider of eSource technology for clinical research, is rolling out AI eSource Builder, a new product that creates an initial draft of a research site's eSource study build from the protocol, supporting documents and site preferences.

Source preparation is a largely invisible bottleneck in clinical trials. In a study published this year by the Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development, at least 80% of sites reported that preparing source documents for high-complexity trials takes more than 21 hours, and 77% said the specialized skills needed to translate protocols into source documents constrain their organizations.

At early adopter sites, AI eSource Builder is saving an average of 4 hours on each study build, and those savings grow over time through a built-in feedback loop. Every finished build, including the changes a site's team makes during review, informs how the builder drafts that site's next study, so each new build starts closer to how the site works. Study designers review and refine every draft, then finalize it in CRIO before it goes live. No build reaches a study without human review.

“Most of the conversation about AI in clinical research is about what it can take off people's plates. The more important question is what it should never take off their plates,” said Jonathan Andrus, Co-CEO, CRIO. “Judgment about how a study runs belongs to site teams, and AI eSource Builder gives them a faster start so they can focus on the areas where their time and expertise are needed most. AI works best when it does one well-defined job well, inside the systems sites already use, with a person reviewing every output.”

Sites upload their protocols along with blank or annotated electronic case report forms (eCRFs) or eCRF completion guidelines. AI eSource Builder reads the Schedule of Assessments and generates an initial version with visits, windows and procedure templates already in place, pulling from both the site's own templates and CRIO's global templates.

Build rules decide how those templates come together. CRIO provides a starting set of 150+ build rules, drawn from its experience supporting thousands of studies, that each site can adjust and extend. The same rules apply across every study, so each new build follows the site's standards no matter who builds it.

“Participating in CRIO’s AI eSource Builder Early Release Program has been a great experience,” says Amber Victor, VP Operations at Elevate Clinical Research, “The builder is intuitive, efficient, and has the potential to significantly reduce the time required to build eSource while improving consistency across our studies.”

AI eSource Builder works only with study design documents, such as protocols and eCRFs, so no electronic protected health information (ePHI) or subject-level data is ever involved. CRIO's agreements with its AI model providers prohibit training on customer data, and models receive only the sections of a document needed for each task.

“Sites and sponsors want to know two things about any AI tool: where their data goes, and who makes the decisions,” said Marc Wartenberger, VP of Compliance & Security, CRIO. “AI eSource Builder was built so both answers are simple. Study documents stay protected, and qualified site staff review, edit and approve every element before anything goes live. The site remains accountable for its source, exactly as it is today.”

AI eSource Builder is the latest step in CRIO's ongoing work to apply AI where it can meaningfully reduce site burden without touching the judgment that belongs to site teams.

“We saw applied AI as a big opportunity to help sites with study builds, and we see even bigger opportunities once a study is running,” said Mike Wenger, Chief Innovation Officer, CRIO. “We're actively building new AI tools that will save sites time and improve data quality throughout the study.”

data.title: IQVIA Launches IQVIA Life Science Models to Help Life Sciences Companies Predict Clinical Trial Outcomes
data.description:
RESEARCH TRIANGLE PARK, N.C. —

October 7, 2026 – IQVIA (NYSE:IQV), a leading global provider of clinical research services, commercial insights and healthcare intelligence to the life sciences and healthcare industries, today at TechIQ 2026 introduced IQVIA Life Science Models™ to help predict clinical trial outcomes.

IQVIA Life Science Models are a suite of purpose-built models for life sciences, combining IQVIA’s proprietary expert content, deep domain knowledge and established regulatory, compliance and privacy frameworks. Built using technologies including NVIDIA Nemotron™ and supported by Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure, the models connect molecular and treatment information with patient journeys and clinical outcomes to enable predictive applications across clinical development. 

  • Clinical study simulation and protocol optimization, including endpoint selection, patient eligibility criteria, dose selection and sample size planning, helping teams identify risks before trials begin. In initial evaluation across 50 trials and 270 endpoints, 85% of predictions were on target or clinically close.
  • Digital twins and synthetic controls that support more efficient study designs. 
  • Leverage clinical study predictions to inform better real-world planning and access.

In clinical development, Life Science Models extend IQVIA’s Predictive Clinical Development approach, enabling sponsors to simulate studies and test key assumptions before execution, helping optimize study design and identify potential risks earlier.

To learn more, visit IQVIA Life Science Models.

data.title: Drugs from China are reshaping biotech. Track the licensing deals here.
data.description:
The makeup of the world’s pharmaceutical pipeline is changing. China’s fast-growing biotechnology industry is a big reason why. 

Over the past decade, China’s government has sought to upgrade the country’s drugmaking capabilities. Its efforts birthed a burgeoning ecosystem of homegrown companies and science parks that mirror — and even rival —  U.S. hubs in Boston and San Francisco. Lower costs and regulatory flexibility have helped China’s biotech startups move faster than their U.S. counterparts, producing a sprawling inventory of drug prospects. While many are designed to be superior versions of medicines either on the market or in development elsewhere, more and more are innovative, challenging the U.S.’s long-held biotech advantage. 

Large pharma companies and venture capital investors have taken note. Many are licensing experimental drugs from China, either to add to their drug portfolios or build new biotechs around. The shift has been rapid, with dealmaking spiking in recent years. According to analysts, licensing agreements hit a record pace in 2025. Fully one-third of the industry’s licensing spending in 2025 involved drugs sourced from China, per the investment bank Jefferies. That trajectory has accelerated in 2026.

These deals reveal important insights about the types of medicines drugmakers and investors want in their portfolios. With this database, we’re tracking deals from 2025 onward in which China-based drugmakers licensed to U.S. and European companies rights to human therapeutics. We show the companies involved, the financial terms of their alliances and details about the medicines and drug targets. 

If we’ve missed a deal, or there’s any additional information you’d like to see, please reach out and let us know.

Licensing deals involving China-developed drugs

Database includes deals announced in 2025 and 2026 that involve a China-based biotechnology firm licensing a drug candidate or candidates to biopharmaceutical companies located in the U.S. or Europe.

Methodology

For this database, BioPharma Dive compiled deals announced in 2025 and 2026 through which China-based drugmakers licensed out innovative human medicines to biotech or pharmaceutical companies in the U.S. or Europe. 

We screened for these deals in company press releases, analyst reports and on social media sites like LinkedIn. We eliminated those that didn’t meet our criteria, including alliances that don’t mention any specific drug candidates or partnerships between two China-based companies. We also excluded deals involving generic drugs or biosimilars.

We generally used a deal’s most advanced program to determine the therapeutic area of focus, treatment type and stage of development at the time of a deal’s announcement. We categorized phase of development by the latest stage underway at the time of a deal.

Therapeutic areas cover a large number of diseases and, in some cases, overlap. In most cases, when companies identified more than one therapeutic area with equal priority, we classified them as working on “multiple” therapeutic areas. Companies that identified multiple areas, but prioritized one over others were classified under that priority area.

Ned Pagliarulo contributed reporting.
